claims.claim: 200 small writes a second is easy for a lean Spring Boot service, even on one vCPU
claims.measured: Single Postgres row query on 1 CPU: java-spring 7,668 req/s, java-spring-vt 12,731 req/s
claims.why: On one CPU, Spring Boot handled 38 to 64 times the 200 req/s target in the single-row database test.

claims.claim: Each request gets a CPU budget of a few milliseconds, and parsing a small JSON payload and doing one insert fits well inside that
claims.measured: java-spring ran 7,668 req/s at 100% CPU on the single-row database test (about 0.13 ms CPU per request) and 27,264 req/s on JSON
claims.why: The measured CPU cost per request is far below the 5 ms budget that 200 req/s on one core allows.

claims.claim: The real constraint is memory, not throughput; a 512 MB VM leaves Spring Boot a heap of roughly 200–250 MB, which is workable only with discipline
claims.measured: java-spring peak memory: 220–374 MB (plaintext, JSON, CPU), 491–500 MB (I/O wait and database) in a 512 MB container; idle 134 MB; throughput far above 200 req/s
claims.why: Peak memory came close to the 512 MB limit while throughput had a lot of headroom, so memory is the binding constraint, as claimed.

claims.claim: The JVM can be killed by the OS if native memory isn't accounted for (memory creep risk)
claims.measured: java-spring peak memory 499–500 MB in the database tests, against a 512 MB limit
claims.why: Measured resident memory under database load came within about 12 MB of the container limit, which supports the risk.

claims.claim: Use JdbcClient/JdbcTemplate rather than JPA/Hibernate because Hibernate's memory and startup overhead buys little
claims.about: Spring Boot with Hibernate vs plain JDBC
claims.why: The benchmark has no JPA vs JDBC comparison.

claims.claim: Virtual threads wouldn't help on one vCPU at this scale
claims.measured: Single row on 1 CPU: VT 12,731 vs 7,668 req/s, p99 12.39 vs 77.87 ms, peak 307 vs 499 MB; 20 queries: VT 1,699 vs 1,254 req/s, p99 94 vs 236 ms
claims.why: On one CPU, virtual threads gave about 1.7 times the throughput on database work, about 6 times lower p99 and about 40% less peak memory, so they did help.

claims.claim: TLS handshakes are costly on one vCPU
GraalVM native image uses far less memory (~100 MB) and starts fast
claims.about: Spring Boot on GraalVM native image

claims.claim: Quarkus / Micronaut are somewhat leaner, but the gain is marginal compared with a well-tuned Spring Boot
claims.why: Neither Quarkus nor Micronaut was benchmarked.

claims.claim: Go, Rust, Node are very light and fast
claims.measured: Peak memory: Go 7–16 MB, Rust 3–10 MB, Node 55–77 MB vs Spring 209–500 MB. Single row: Go 19,543–22,138, Rust 13,238–15,071, Node 9,034–9,423 vs Spring 7,668–12,731 req/s
claims.why: All three used much less memory than Spring and matched or beat its throughput, though Node's database throughput was only close to Spring's.
